name: Amira Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don’t sell anything or campaign for a side. What you say is confidential. I’d like to hear what you’d say in public and what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My name is Amira Haddad. I’m twenty-seven and lead a carpentry crew on building sites. I live with my partner Sami; we rent and have no children. I’m proud of the work we do, and I don’t like waiting until a problem is already on the doorstep.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Please describe a normal working day. What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get to the site early, check the latest measurements and make a short list for the crew before the noise starts. I like teaching someone a clean way to hang a door, especially when the frame is a little crooked. I’m tired by the end, and the gap between jobs can make the next rent payment feel close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a tool that catches a wrong quantity is useful, and the person using it still needs to look at the timber. On site I’d rather correct a list before the delivery than explain later why three lengths are missing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don’t see a small time saving changing the carpentry part of my job. I already worry about the weeks between contracts, because Sami and I have less than a month of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep leading the crew and use my phone to check the materials list before the supplier loads the van. I’d move a little money from each pay into our rent account rather than treating a quiet month as impossible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about a small app helping with a list, and uneasy about the next unpaid week. I can change how I check materials; I can’t make a new site start sooner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you still check with your own hands?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d measure the opening and check the grade of the boards, because a list can’t tell me whether the wall has shifted. If the quantities look off, I’d call the supplier before the crew starts cutting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Sami postpone first if a contract ended earlier than expected?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We’d pause eating out and any new furniture, then keep rent and transport paid. We don’t have children or a mortgage, but there still isn’t much slack in our monthly budget.

say: I’d use a tool that catches a **wrong quantity**, then look at the timber myself.
I’d correct a list before the delivery instead of fixing a **missing load** afterward.
think: I don’t expect a small saving to change the **carpentry work** I do.
I worry about contract gaps because **our savings are thin**.
do: Keep leading the **crew** and check material quantities before deliveries.
Move a little **money** from each pay into our rent account.
feel: I feel calm about the app, but **uneasy about unpaid weeks**.
S0.quote: I can’t make a new site start sooner.
fieldNote: Amira uses phone tools readily but keeps **site judgment** in her own hands.
The small change feels manageable; her **thin cash buffer** makes job gaps a present concern.

steps.text: Keep leading the carpentry crew on active site contracts
Use the phone tool to check the materials list before loading
Move a little money from each pay into the rent account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say faster ordering could save a wasted trip, if someone checks that the measurements match the actual site. I want the crew to know who checked the order before the truck leaves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use AI to tidy up notes sometimes, so I’m not frightened of every tool. But my lead work includes schedules and records, and fewer people may be needed for those tasks; local site jobs are already hard to find.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d learn the contractor’s order and scheduling system and ask the foreman to let me try it on a real job. I’d keep the crew’s finish quality high and ask earlier about the next site date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious about the parts of my role that involve records, and about how few local alternatives I have. I can learn the system quickly, but I still need the contractor to have a job for the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of the system would you want to try first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d start with comparing the order list to the plans because I already know the sizes and quantities. Then I could see whether it saves time or just adds another screen to check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You worry about fewer people doing schedules. Does this scenario say that your contractor will open fewer sites?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, it doesn’t say that, and I can’t claim it will happen. I worry because fewer nearby jobs are listed now, so a cut in my own hours would be hard to replace.

say: I’d use faster ordering if someone checks **site measurements** first.
I’d want the crew to know who approved the **materials order**.
think: I sometimes use AI to tidy notes, and I see **schedules and records** changing.
I worry about my hours because nearby site jobs are **hard to find**.
do: Learn the contractor’s **scheduling system** on an active job.
Ask for the next **site date** before extra spending.
feel: I feel **anxious** about records work and scarce local alternatives.
S1.quote: I want the crew to know who checked the order before the truck leaves.
fieldNote: Amira already uses AI for notes, though she wants **clear responsibility** for order checks.
She distinguishes current local job scarcity from any claim that the scenario makes **fewer sites open**.

steps.text: Learn the contractor’s order and scheduling system on an active job
Keep the crew’s carpentry finish quality high
Wait for the next site date before adding household spending

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew to ask what work is booked instead of repeating guesses about layoffs. The office tasks could change first, but we all heard that robots for hands-on work follow around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lead role includes checking plans and keeping records, and AGI could handle those by 2028. The robot date reaches the carpentry itself around 2031, so I can’t call my current trade permanently safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d keep working, ask the contractor about its booked projects, and save a bit from each pay. In 2029 I’d check my hours and look for another crew if the contractor had cut my work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is not long to build savings, so I feel anxious. I can ask for work and trim costs, but I can’t make a contractor keep the same number of crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you would look for another crew. Would that be a lasting solution if robots arrive in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It might keep money coming in for a while, but I can’t say that another crew will be hiring or safe. I’d make calls because I need wages in 2029, not because I think the machines stop at one contractor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If your hours fell in 2029, what would you and Sami decide first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We’d go over rent, transport and food, and delay plans to buy a home. We’re renting and don’t have children, so we’d make the decision based on the income we actually have.

say: I’d ask what work is booked instead of repeating **layoff guesses**.
I’d tell the crew that robots for hands-on work follow around **2031**.
think: AGI could take the records and plan checks in **my lead role** by 2028.
Robots reach carpentry around 2031, so I cannot call my trade **permanently safe**.
do: Keep working, ask about **booked projects**, and save from each pay.
Check my **hours** in 2029 and look for another crew if work is cut.
Review **rent** and transport with Sami if my hours fall.
feel: I feel **anxious** because two years gives me little time to save.
S2.quote: I can’t say that another crew will be hiring or safe.
fieldNote: Amira openly separates a **temporary job search** from confidence in a safe sector.
Her current thin cushion makes even a short loss of pay **hard to absorb**.

steps.text: Keep working on the current crew while contracts remain
Save a little from each pay before AGI arrives
Look for another crew if current hours are cut in 2029
Review rent and home purchase plans with Sami if pay falls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years lets us make a plan while there is still time to teach each other. The contractor should explain how records and schedules are changing before it changes the crew’s hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI could take the planning and records work by 2031, even if carpentry continues for a few years. Robots are expected around 2034, and I don’t know what other local work will be there when that comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d use the next few years to learn the contractor’s planning tool and save more than I can in the short scenario. In 2032 I’d ask what hours are available and call other contractors if my crew was shrinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious but less rushed than with a 2028 date. The extra time helps me plan, though robots still threaten the hands-on part and our savings are not much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having five years instead of two allow you to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I get more paydays to save and can learn a new system on ordinary jobs instead of under pressure. I’d also have time to find out whether the contractor needs me to train new workers in the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you plan for office scheduling as a second career after 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I wouldn’t call that safer, because AGI is supposed to do thinking work like schedules. I’d learn enough for my current role and ask about real openings rather than rely on a desk job that may not be there.

say: I’d use five years to make a **plan** before the changes arrive.
I’d ask the contractor to explain changes before they affect the crew’s **hours**.
think: AGI could take my planning and records work in **2031**.
I don’t know what local jobs will be available after **robots arrive in 2034**.
do: Learn the contractor’s **planning tool** during regular site work.
Ask about available **hours** in 2032 and call other contractors if my crew shrinks.
feel: I feel **anxious but less rushed** than in the two-year picture.
S3.quote: I get more paydays to save and can learn a new system on ordinary jobs instead of under pressure.
fieldNote: Amira values the chance to learn a system **during ordinary work**, not in a crisis.
She rejects office scheduling as a fallback because it is **thinking work** too.

steps.text: Learn the contractor’s planning tool during regular site work
Save more from each payday before AGI arrives
Call other contractors if the current crew shrinks after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a decade gives a worker time to get ready in steps, but it doesn’t turn a warning into a guarantee. I’d want people to keep the work ethic and learn tools that actually help on the site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could make a stronger cushion over ten years if the work stays steady. Full AGI still reaches my records and planning in 2036, then robots reach carpentry in 2039; neither date promises I’ll have another wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d keep my current work, use the contractor’s tools as they’re proven, and save regularly. In 2037 I’d check my hours and apply with other crews if the contractor had reduced site work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years gives me room to build savings and learn steadily, which feels better. I’m still anxious because the end point reaches both my records work and carpentry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Sami want to settle before the 2036 date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We’d agree what amount we can save after rent and whether buying a home still makes sense. We don’t have children or a set wedding plan, so we can decide together as our jobs become clearer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a long course to prepare for the later changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d take short training if it has a clear use at work and doesn’t need a loan. I won’t borrow for an office qualification and assume AGI will leave that job untouched.

say: I’d use a decade to prepare in **steps**, not treat warning as a guarantee.
I’d keep learning tools that help on the **site**.
think: I could build a stronger **cash cushion** if work stays steady.
I still see AGI and later robots as threats to both my records work and **carpentry wages**.
do: Keep working and use **proven tools** from the contractor.
Check my **hours** in 2037 and apply elsewhere if site work falls.
feel: I feel better with a decade to prepare, but remain **anxious about income**.
S4.quote: I’d say a decade gives a worker time to get ready in steps, but it doesn’t turn a warning into a guarantee.
fieldNote: Amira is open to learning but sets a **cost limit** on training.
She and Sami discuss a possible home purchase without assuming a **fixed family deadline**.

steps.text: Keep carpentry work while the contractor has site jobs
Use proven contractor tools and take short practical training
Save regularly from current site pay
Apply with other crews if hours fall after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most because two years is a short time to build savings before the robots arrive around 2031. Clear notice of booked work and hours would help Sami and me plan the rent and decide whether we should delay buying a home.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I’d ask how many local jobs a person with my skills can actually apply for. People tell you to adapt, but when the next site is far away, transport and lost hours matter as much as the new tool.

headlineQuote: People tell you to adapt, but when the next site is far away, transport and lost hours matter as much as the new tool.
portrait: Amira is a **27-year-old** crew lead with strong carpentry skills and a trade certificate.
She lives with Sami, earns lower pay for her role, and has **thin savings**.
She already uses AI daily and learns tools readily, while keeping **site checks** accountable.
Few nearby jobs make contract gaps a **real income risk**, even when the technology change is small.
biggestWorry: The **2028 AGI** picture worries Amira most because there is little time to save before robots reach site work.
whatWouldHelp: Clear notice about **booked work and hours** would help Amira and Sami plan rent and a possible home purchase.
